aspects.says: A record has no no-arg constructor and its fields can't be written by reflection, so a binder must pass the values, matched by component name and type, to the canonical constructor, which runs the record's own checks.
basis: section:A Binder Can Build a Record Only Through Its Canonical Constructor

aspects.says: A record's equals and hashCode are derived from its component list, so a component added later is part of equality at once, while a hand-written class's equals and hashCode drift and treat different keys as equal.
basis: section:A Record's equals and hashCode Follow Its Component List, So a New Field Can't Be Left Out

aspects.says: An array component is compared by identity, toString prints every component, and the generated hashCode's algorithm is unspecified.
aspects.reason: lookup facts gathered in the Reference table; the page argues none of them, and a practice on them would test recall of the table

aspects.says: Turning a JavaBean DTO without equals into a record changes its equality from identity to values, so sets and maps that kept equal beans apart now merge them.
basis: section:Moving a JavaBean DTO to a Record Turns Identity into Value Equality

aspects.says: Adding a component makes every canonical-constructor call and record pattern written for the old header a compile error, while accessor calls still compile.
basis: section:Adding a Component Breaks Every Constructor Call and Record Pattern at Compile Time

aspects.says: A record is only shallowly immutable: a mutable collection component changed after the record became a map key changes its hash and loses the entry, unless the compact constructor stores an unmodifiable copy rather than a view.
basis: section:A Record Is Only Shallowly Immutable: a List Component Can Change Under a Map Key
